title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance (Canonical)
author: Evelyn Park
content:
Purpose

This canonical standards document consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It is a reference for architects, platform engineers, and service owners to ensure consistent, reliable, and maintainable services.

Scope

Applies to all services that expose public or internal Redwood inference APIs, model-serving components (hosted / dedicated / private), and platform infrastructure owned by engineering. Exclusions: experimental prototypes and research notebooks (place those in team Google Drive).

Principles

- Developer-first: clear APIs, fast feedback loops, and excellent DX for SDK / REST consumers.
- Production-first: prioritize observability, reliability, and graceful degradation.
- Cost-aware: prefer designs that improve unit economics (batching, caching, quantization).
- Reproducible and auditable: deployments must be automatable and traceable through CI and the control plane.

1) API Standards

Overview:
- API surface should be stable, well-documented, and versioned. Use OpenAPI 3.1 for all public and partner-facing endpoints.

Key rules:
- Versioning: path-based major versions (/v1/...), with semantic compatibility guarantees for minor changes. Backward-compatible additions (optional fields) do not increment major version.
- Idempotency: write endpoints must accept an Idempotency-Key header for client retries.
- Auth: OAuth2 bearer tokens for external consumers; mTLS + JWT for internal service-to-service calls. Document required scopes per endpoint.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for list endpoints. Avoid offset-based pagination for large result sets.
- Error model: Use structured errors with fields {code, message, details}. Provide well-documented HTTP status mappings: 400 (validation), 401 (auth), 403 (forbidden), 404 (not found), 429 (rate limit), 500 (internal).
- Rate limiting: per-API-key token bucket. Default tier: 1000 req/min per project (adjustable via account tier). Return standard Retry-After header on 429.
- Streaming: support chunked transfer for streaming generation; provide final completion event. Clients that request streaming must include ?stream=true.

Examples:
- Generation request (simplified): POST /v1/generate
  Headers: Authorization: Bearer <token>, Idempotency-Key: <key>
  Body: {"model": "redwood-v2", "input": "Write a short summary...", "max_tokens": 256}
- Structured error example: {"code":"generation_timeout","message":"Model did not respond within 30s","details": {"request_id":"req_123"}}

Backward compatibility checklist for changes:
1. Additive fields only? OK.
2. Remove or rename fields? Requires major version or appropriate adapter.
3. Behavioral changes (defaults, validation)? Must be documented and coordinated with SDK owners.

2) Coding Standards

Languages & repositories:
- Primary languages: Go (services & runtime control plane), Rust (latency-critical runtime kernels), Python (tools, evals, SDK), TypeScript (console & SDK).
- Monorepo vs services: Service teams decide repository strategy but must follow CI rules below.

Style & quality gates:
- Linting: golangci-lint (Go), clippy (Rust), flake8/black (Python), eslint/prettier (TS). Lint failures are CI-blocking.
- Testing: unit tests ~> 80% critical path coverage; integration tests required for API contracts and model-serving components. Use test subsets in CI to keep feedback fast.
- Type safety: prefer static typing for public interfaces. All public Go/Rust APIs must include API-level docs and examples.
- Code reviews: minimum 1 owner review + 1 cross-team reviewer for infra-affecting changes.

3) Infrastructure Standards

IaC and environment segregation:
- All deployable infra must be defined in Terraform (modules under eng-infra/terraform). No manual changes to production resources outside CI.
- Environments: dev, staging, prod. Staging must mirror prod networking and data protection.

CI/CD:
- Pipeline: PR -> unit tests & linters -> canary deploy to staging -> automated smoke tests -> promote to prod.
- Canary policy: default 5% of traffic for 15 minutes with automated health checks (latency, error-rate).

Secrets & keys:
- Store secrets in KMS-backed secret manager (cloud KMS or HSM for Private deployments). Audit log every secret access.

Capacity & autoscaling:
- Default autoscale policy for inference services: target CPU utilization 60% / GPU utilization 70% with headroom for sudden bursts.
- Multi-region: active-active for critical services; failover documented for region outages.

4) Model-serving Standards

Model packaging & versioning:
- Every deployable model artifact must have a model manifest: {model_id, semantic_version, quantization_profile_id, input_schema_hash, build_artifact_sha}.
- Model version promotion: dev -> canary -> prod. Canary runs must expose the same metrics and tracing as prod.

Execution & runtime rules:
- Batch sizing: default max batch per GPU = 32 for decoding-heavy models; dynamic batching algorithm should aim for target latency SLOs.
- KV cache: support per-request KV cache policies. Default TTL = 5 minutes for prefix caching; configurable by route.
- Quantization: maintain a quantization profile registry; each profile must include expected delta in quality metrics vs FP16 baseline (e.g., -0.5% BLEU).
- Fallbacks: runtime must support model variant fallback (e.g., fp16 -> int8) and region fallback with circuit-breakers.

Model governance & evals:
- Every model promoted to prod must have an evaluation report with: quality metrics (task-specific), regression test set pass/fail, adversarial checks, and privacy/data-leak scanning.
- Rollout gating: automatic rollback if model introduces >3% regression on critical evals or increases error budget burn rate beyond configured threshold.

Model-serving config table (default values):
| Deployment Tier | Default Autoscale | Max Batch Size | KV Cache TTL | Latency SLO (p95) |
|-----------------|-------------------|----------------|--------------|-------------------|
| Hosted (api)    | target GPU 70%    | 16             | 300s         | 300ms             |
| Dedicated       | target GPU 75%    | 32             | 600s         | 250ms             |
| Private         | configurable      | 32             | 600s         | customer-defined  |

5) Observability Standards

Metrics & dashboards:
- Metrics: all services must emit Prometheus-format metrics (service_*, api_*, model_*). Key metrics: request_latency_seconds_bucket, request_errors_total, tokens_generated_total, model_load_time_seconds, batch_size_distribution.
- SLOs: define SLOs at the route and model level in the console. Default objective examples: availability 99.95% (monthly), latency p95 < 300ms for generation (hosted).
- Dashboards: per-service dashboards (latency, errors, cost breakdown), per-model dashboards (latency, tokens, quality regressions).

Tracing & logs:
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry distributed tracing for all inbound requests. Trace ID must be propagated through model-serving RPCs and included in structured logs.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, request_id, trace_id, route, user_id (when available but PII-scrubbed).

Alerts & on-call:
- Alert categories: SLO burn, infra capacity, deployment failures, security incidents. Alerts MUST include runbooks and expected mitigation steps.
- On-call: every service must have a primary on-call roster listed in eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts.

6) Performance Standards & Benchmarking

Latency & throughput targets:
- Short generation endpoints (<=128 tokens): p95 < 300ms, p99 < 1.2s.
- Long generation endpoints (>512 tokens): throughput target expressed as tokens/sec per GPU; example baseline: 75 tokens/sec for redwood-v2-large at FP16 on A100.
- Embeddings: p95 < 150ms, p99 < 600ms.

Benchmarking methodology:
- Synthetic benchmarks: use representative prompt sets from prompt-sets-and-benchmarks. Run continuous benchmarks in eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite.
- Load tests: stage before major releases. Run 3-week soak tests for autoscaling policy changes.
- Reporting: publish benchmark results to the Console and related product pages; include hardware profile and kernel flags.

7) ADRs (Decision Records)

All architecture changes that affect cross-team behavior should have an ADR. ADRs must include: context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences, and owners. Key ADRs (examples):
- ADR-2025-07: Kernel selection strategy (prefer vendor kernels w/ validated perf profiles).
- ADR-2025-11: Model artifact versioning format (semantic + build sha).
- ADR-2026-01: Default streaming protocol (chunked HTTP + event markers).

ADR process:
1. Draft ADR in eng repo under /decisions with a short RFC.
2. Review by architecture-and-standards reviewers.
3. Publish to Confluence and link to related code/config.

8) Change and Review Cadence

- Standards review: architecture-and-standards group holds a quarterly review of canonical standards and updates.
- Emergency exceptions: for production safety issues, a fast-path exception is allowed but requires documented retrospective and follow-up ADR.

9) Onboarding Checklist for New Service Owners

- Create OpenAPI spec and publish to the API registry.
- Implement authentication and Idempotency handling.
- Add Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry traces.
- Create dashboards and SLOs in Console.
- Add CI checks, linting, and integration tests.
- Run benchmark and fill model-serving manifest (if applicable).

Appendix: Quick Reference Cheatsheet

- OpenAPI for all public endpoints.
- Idempotency-Key header for mutating calls.
- Prometheus + OpenTelemetry for metrics & traces.
- Model manifest required for every model.
- Canary default: 5% for 15 minutes with rollback gates.
